title: AmpereBleed: Exploiting On-chip Current Sensors for Circuit-Free Attacks on ARM-FPGA SoCs
problem: FPGAs are vulnerable to power side-channel attacks; existing attacks require assumptions of co-resident crafted circuits and shared power delivery networks, limiting practicality.
motivation: FPGA adoption in cloud multi-tenancy exposes shared power delivery to side-channel threats; removal of attack assumptions is critical for real-world security.
method: AmpereBleed exploits INA226 current sensors—measurement devices built into ARM-FPGA SoCs (chips combining ARM processors and programmable logic on one die)—in a power side-channel attack (stealing secrets by observing electrical usage patterns). By reading what these sensors measure, attackers can fingerprint (identify by their unique electrical signatures) what encryption and machine-learning programs are executing, then exploit that knowledge to extract their secrets. Unlike earlier power side-channel attacks, this one doesn't require planting malicious circuits on the chip first; it uses only sensors the manufacturer already included.
key_novelty: A power side-channel attack—stealing secrets by observing electrical power usage—that uses only the built-in INA226 current sensors to spy on machine-learning and encryption programs, without needing to plant malicious circuits on the chip.
contributions: AmpereBleed attack achieving 261x greater signal variations vs ring oscillator techniques
DNN model fingerprinting on Xilinx Deep Learning Processor Unit (DPU) with 99.7% accuracy
RSA-1024 key Hamming weight distinction capability

metrics.speedup: 261x greater signal variation vs ring oscillator

limitations: Not discussed—no analysis of attack detection or mitigation feasibility.
primary_theme: Circuit-free power side-channel attack via current sensors
